transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Radei.
I'm your host, Eripalmian, and with me in the studio is my friend and colleague Nick
Klassevos.
How are you?
I'm all good.
I mean yesterday we finished the annual Cert of Requires conference, which was
fantastic, so I feel great today.
Today we are excited to have David Marcus on the show.
David is a US investor with strong connections to Europe and Sweden.
And David is also an entertaining person full of fascinating insights and
stories from his decades in financial markets, so this will be fun.
Which book will we speak about?
So David has selected how to make a few billion dollars written by Brad Jacobs.
And the Jacobs is a serial entrepreneur who have built a number of billion dollar
companies through an acquisition driven approach.
How to make a few billion dollars was published in 2024.
And we are thrilled to speak about the book today.
Here comes our conversation with David Marcus.
Hi David and welcome to investing by the books podcast.
It's great to be here.
It's our pleasure and wonderful to have you on.
Last time we met was in New York, 2022.
We had dinner there.
This week we had the pleasure to have you at the conference to see the
queries conference in Stockholm.
How do you feel now?
I feel good.
I really liked the conference.
It was the first time I went.
I really liked it.
I met a lot of companies and a lot of the people that attended.
And so I learned a lot and I got to see a lot.
And I have a lot to think about now as a result.
And for those not familiar with you, how was your background?
How did you get into investing in the first place?
Long we have to go back in time quite quite a ways.
I guess I'll give the quick version, but I was very lucky.
I grew up in a house in New York, in Long Island, where my
father and my uncle owned a two-man stock brokerage firm.
And they talked about stocks all the time.
And so I was always around the discussions of investing and finding
interesting companies.
In those days, they were always talking about finding the next IBM
or the next Xerox, those were the big ones of those days.
And even when I was a kid, I would ask them,
why aren't you buying IBM or Xerox?
Why do you need the next one?
So there was always a debate in the discussion about companies.
And then one day my uncle took me to the New York Stock Exchange,
where you could go to a visitor's gallery and oversee the exchange.
And at that point, it was, I would say to me,
it was the center of the financial universe.
It was just incredible.
So I was hooked from that minute.
I knew I really wanted to be somehow connected to investing.
And how long were you done?
I was probably 14.
So then I started subscribing to magazines like Fortune Magazine
and Forbes.
Yes, other kids were interested in different kinds of magazines.
And not me.
And so I did that.
And I would read anything I could find on the stock market,
how it worked, who the players were.
But I was always fascinated by the history of it.
So I would find old books about the people from 80 years ago,
100 years ago, and how they did it.
And I just wanted to learn and read a lot.
And were you allowed to invest anything?
Yeah.
And so just, I would track,
I guess that I would speak to my own father and my uncle about it.
And I just wanted to read about the companies.
And we would pick companies.
And I realized even then I liked conglomerates and holding companies.
And I remember one of the first stocks that I picked myself
was a company called Gulf and Western.
And Gulf and Western was a crazy conglomerate.
It doesn't exist anymore.
But their biggest asset was Paramount Pictures,
the movie studio, which has subsequently been sold quite a few times.
And so, and then the corporate raiders.
So there are these guys that would attack these conglomerates
and push them to break up and sell off all the pieces.
And so I would just track them and watch those guys.
And I realized there's so much value in these conglomerates
because the investors don't know how to look at them or how to value them.
So over time, I just really started thinking about big companies
that just had a lot of different kinds of businesses, old industrial businesses.
And because even then, so at that point I wasn't 14 anymore.
I was older, but I realized that investors were shifting more towards
companies that did specific sectors or industries.
And kind of they forgot about these other ones.
But they were very asset rich.
So these, these corporate raiders would come in and try to take control
and push them to break up.
So for university, I went to a school in Boston called Northeastern University.
It really was a great place to go because it helped me.
It was a five year under, so in the US most schools are four years for university.
This is a five year school because when you, but it's still four years of education
because you go there.
And during the five years, you have to get a job.
You have to interview.
You learn how to interview.
You compete against other students.
It's very competitive.
And you work, you work six months full time, three times over the course of the five years.
And so when you graduate, you have actual real experience working.
And I was very lucky that I worked at a bank in Boston
that did the back office for a, he wasn't well known at the time,
but who became an extremely well known Wall Street guy,
who really was my first real boss on Wall Street.
And that was Michael Price, who I worked for for many years.
And so the bank recommended me to him.
And in 1987, I worked right around the corner from the New York Stock Exchange.
And so, but in that year, there was a stock market crash.
So in the US, there was a massive crash, I think.
And one day, the, I think the stock exchange was down 22% in one day.
My job was answering the phone.
I, investors would call, it was a mutual fund company.
I think at the time it had maybe just under two billion dollars
was one of the largest mutual funds in the United States.
And Michael was sort of just coming up as a, as a well known investor, as a value investor,
but also a creative investor.
He wasn't just picking stocks that he liked, but he liked the deals when they were,
a lot of mergers in those days, and they would play these arbitrage spreads
between the announced deal price and where the stocks were trading.
And so, you could, most investors after a deal was announced,
the stock would go up, but not to the full price,
because it would take time for the deal to close.
And he would buy it then sometimes, and then just play that spread
on an annualized basis. Sometimes it was a very high rate of return.
And so, that became a whole industry that a lot of people started to do,
but he was so early in that kind of investing.
And so, when the crash happened, it kind of was a big disruption.
But I got to watch him and the rest of the team and how they operated during a crisis.
They didn't panic. They didn't go crazy.
They just sat back, watched the carnage, and thought,
how can we take advantage of this?
And so, it was one of the earliest lessons for me,
which was crisis can create opportunity if you don't panic.
It doesn't mean you have to start buying things the first minute of the crisis,
but it's a period of time where when everybody's panicking, if you are rational,
you can see that people, in the panic, people start throwing everything away.
They want to get out of everything. They're selling the good ones, the bad ones.
It doesn't matter. They just want to get out.
And their viewers will worry about getting back in at some point,
if we ever get back in.
So, you just realize...
So, that was such a valuable lesson where I was just in my early 20s at that point.
So, it was a good kickoff.
And then I just wanted to work in the business.
So, the person who had started the company was an older guy,
who had come to the US from Germany in the 1930s,
Max Heina, and Michael worked for him and trained under him.
And that guy had really developed a skill that he would look at bonds that were defaulted.
But they had a lot of assets.
And so, that he helped train Michael to look at all the footnotes and all the bond indentures.
Because most people didn't look at these things.
And they realized these were very asset-rich companies,
even though they had no cash flow.
So, they were in bankruptcy.
But when they started selling assets, people could get enormous returns.
So, you were buying bonds at 10 or 20 cents on the dollar.
And at the end, they paid more than 100 cents in a dollar,
because they paid the full amount.
And then they paid the interest that had accrued for many years.
And so, there were a lot of these interesting companies going through big bankruptcies, really, in the US.
Most of the railroads went out of business.
The government took them over.
And so, again, so he learned crisis-crease opportunity.
He trained us to learn that as well.
And so, you're forever learning.
I think that's the reality of it.
And you weren't scared off of the crisis that came so early
and situation you were in.
Was that because Michael and the other people in the team
that they didn't freak out in that episode you think were?
I think it was helpful, for sure.
To see everybody outside was freaking out.
We were already getting lots of phone calls from investors.
But one day, it was investors who wanted to invest in the fund.
The next week, it was investors who wanted to get out of the fund,
because they were panicking.
Well, the way the system worked in those days, you could add to your investment on the phone.
You couldn't take your money out on the phone.
You had to send in a letter.
You had to get it stamped in a bank to confirm your signature.
And people didn't realize that told the crisis.
And so, it was more panic.
What do you mean I can't sell it today?
And so it was eventually that change, especially with technology and internet
and you could do everything online, but that came years later.
But yes, they were calm during the storm.
Even though his fund was down a lot he just focused on how can I take advantage.
And so, it was great to get those lessons early in your career.
If everything just works for you right away,
then when something bad happens you have no experience in it.
I think it's better to see the problems,
because it really helps you understand what can go wrong.
You learn it. You learn a lot.
You learn more.
Sometimes you learn more from the crisis, the mistakes, the problems.
Then you do from the successes, because it helps you avoid.
It's like getting the map to the minefield.
You know what to avoid.
You know where the issues are.
We will speak more about your career and what has happened since then.
But for this episode we will speak about a book.
And you mentioned the successes.
And I think this is a pretty successful story.
How to make a few billion dollars is the title.
Pretty humble title.
How did you first come across the book?
Well, I had heard about Brad Jacobs who wrote the book.
It's his autobiography.
Because he was such a prolific business builder.
He was a serial entrepreneur.
And so he would make many acquisitions.
But he would stick to one sector in a company.
Make a lot of acquisitions.
List.
It would be a listed company.
And then he would build another one.
And maybe a peripheral or nearby sector.
But not necessarily the same industry.
And it wasn't just creating sort of a serial acquireer across industries.
It was a serial acquireer in a specific industry.
But then he would build another company.
And another one.
And another one.
And I think the largest one is United Rentals.
That's a global business.
I think it's a $50 billion company today market cap.
And he built it from nothing and made hundreds of acquisitions.
So in any case, I had already known who he was.
And I just happened to be at an event where he was the keynote.
And I heard him speaking.
I thought he was like the title of the book, a bit humble.
Now he has a lot to be proud of what he's achieved.
And so he talked about the businesses he built.
But he started talking about the business he wanted to build.
In other words, his next one.
And it was the conference.
That was just over one year ago.
And so he, and at the time the book had just come out.
And they were giving it out at the commerce.
Well, I like that.
I'm a value investor.
Pretty book is never a bad thing.
And it was autographed.
And so but I listened to him and he was talking about this idea to build a company
that would focus on the building products industry.
So he would look for fragmented industries with a lot of small players.
Raise capital and then make a good sized acquisition.
But then layer on other ones on top of the foundation of the big acquisition.
But the way he spoke about how he built businesses.
I thought this is fantastic.
And I guess we'll get into that in a minute.
But the reality is I said, OK, I don't want to just get a free book.
I actually want to read it and understand it because here's somebody who has built
more than five companies that are multi-billion dollar businesses.
He's in his, I think he's 67 or 68 years old.
He's not an old guy.
And he had already achieved so much.
And yet what did he want to do?
Another one.
And so, and I think out of the five companies he started from scratch,
two of them had spin-offs that became multi-billion dollar.
So effectively, he built seven multi-billion dollar companies,
really absolutely remarkable.
And so, yeah, I started focusing on trying to consume as much information on him and understand it.
But frankly, then pretty quickly I reached out to his group.
And just said, hey, I subbride present.
And I am really interested to know more about what you're talking about
because they were going to be raising money for the next idea.
So yes, so this book, and in the book, it's going back to the book.
He highlights his start as just a kid who had a few thousand dollars.
I remember he said, he saw something on some television show about oil traders in Europe,
how they were becoming these incredible, incredibly wealthy guys
because they were trading oil during all these oil crisis periods that were happening in the 1970s.
And he said, oh, I should become an oil trade.
He was like 22 or 23 years old.
He said he didn't know anything about it.
And he talks about that in the book.
And he took the few dollars he had, few thousand dollars.
And somehow he set up some oil trading business that eventually became a large business.
So even early on, he was just wired to succeed.
He just had to drive the passion.
And if he didn't know it, he learned it.
He wasn't waiting for somebody to teach him how to do something.
He decided he would do it himself.
But in the book, he talks about how early on he was focused on business,
but he was also into music.
And he debated to be a musician and not go for the gold or the business guy.
And eventually he chose to go to be the more of the capitalist.
But maybe he came out of the success he had.
And it just pulled him into that area.
But over the years now, you see how much he has built.
And when you meet him, talk to him, see him.
He's done some quite a few interviews.
You just see the passion, the drive.
You see it with some of the serial acquires that I saw at your conference.
And that we know exist.
And when you see that, you kind of want to be part of it.
And as long as you think you could also, I'll say, ride along with them.
Not every business builder is taking the shareholders with them.
Some of them do other things to the shareholders that are not good.
But no.
And in his businesses.
And I mean, in the book, he highlights sort of these, these points,
which is finding just, finding sectors that are.
He started with the oil business, but then he moved on to other businesses.
And then eventually he got into this role of rolling up certain industries.
But he would target businesses and sectors where there were a lot of players.
There were very fragmented industries.
And there was no real main leadership.
Maybe there were a lot of, as we would call it, mom and pops, right.
There were family on smaller businesses.
Or if they were more groups that didn't have a main owner,
they still were just maybe more modest size.
And they'd go and get one.
It creates the base.
And then add the others on it.
So as opposed to some of the cereal acquires that all that want to keep a lot of these acquisitions.
Sort of unique and let them run and manage the way they are.
The model he had was on top of the foundation.
The new one should be adopt, let's adopt a lot of technology.
Let's modernize it.
Let's take advantage of the trends and technologies, one of the key points.
And understand that the people and he was very people focused, technology focused, opportunity focused.
But layer on the new business, the new acquisitions on top of the platform that they were building.
So that it was a unified strategy instead of 50 or 80 or 90 different acquisitions.
So it's just a different model.
I don't, I wouldn't say it's better or worse than any other model.
But for what he was building to build specific companies for specific industries,
it was an excellent model.
So United Rentals, they rolled up the rental equipment market.
Heavy equipment, lighter equipment for back hose and diggers and whatever, all kinds of equipment.
And because every town had a rental company or actually in a lot of cases,
the larger construction companies would buy the equipment for big projects.
And they had all the equipment left over till they had another project.
And so they realized there was a huge opportunity in building rental businesses.
So they were smaller businesses and then they turned it into an actual real vibrant growing productive business.
That's why it's been so successful globally, it's not just the US business, it's around the world.
David, as you said, Jacob's has a different way of running things than the typical Swedish serial acquireer.
And he emphasizes integration, synergies, centralizing certain function,
doing some larger deals, as you mentioned, to build that platform.
Do you think sort of the Swedes can learn from the model that Jacob's had?
Do you think they could sort of add their model in any way using his framework?
Well, it depends on what their business is because we have seen here so many interesting companies
that they buy the business, they love the people who build them and the quality of the business.
And they have no interest in changing it.
They want to keep it unique.
Look, that's frankly Warren Buffett does that, right?
So he has kind of two buckets where he buys a whole business and then he has where he has investments in the stock market,
where that's maybe a buy and one day a sell, where the acquired companies, he's going to keep him forever.
He says he's not going to sell them.
And so the same here in Sweden with groups that are doing similar, where they buy the whole thing,
they're not looking for turnaround, they're not looking for things that can be fixed.
They're not private equity guys thinking let's buy it and the first thing we do is get rid of management.
And we know better than them.
Well, aren't you attracted to it because you like what they do?
So why do you want to start making?
How do you know better than the guy's doing it?
Unless it's a company where it's been undermanaged and it is fixable and you can create more value out of it.
That's not the business that many of the cereal acquires in Sweden are doing.
They're buying good businesses, whether it's Lifco, Rocco, we could go through the list.
They're not looking for trouble, they're looking for great or very good at least that can operate on their own.
But yet the founders of those are willing to sell whether they're retiring or whatever the reason is.
And so both models can work out.
And so for certain kinds of yes, I think the way Bry Jacobs does it, it does work.
He's proved it works.
So it's not just a U.S. thing.
It can work anywhere.
But but some of the cereal acquires, I think they also they will roll up in some of the verticals around.
So they're buying different businesses, but then they could have add-ons.
And those add-ons sometimes are smaller.
They'll go into an existing business.
But they're not really platform companies where they're saying we need ten more like this.
Because most of the cereal acquires are ridiculously opportunistic.
And but and just I think one more thing on or however many more things you want to talk about Bry Jacobs.
But it's he sets very high goals and targets. Why?
I think you could simply say you aim high so that you could land high.
If you aim low, it's hard to aim to land high.
So they set these crazy targets.
And then they have to do everything possible to get to those targets.
But then he rewards his people.
They get equity.
They get all kinds of incentives.
And so he seems to be a I'll say a tough leader of the businesses.
But he wants to bring everybody with him.
Meaning if you're a real contributor in his companies, you get very well rewarded.
And so you see people that are in his group tend to be there.
I'm sure it's very tough and I'm sure it's not easy to be there through especially downturns in those industries and so forth.
Because you know you have to deliver so but they become very seasoned.
And the more seasoned the people are turns out you want the skill sets.
And some of those people can help in the next industry or in the next business that's created.
And so you see some of the people end up in multiple businesses there.
You could track how they move around to the boards or to the businesses.
But setting these huge targets and these huge goals.
I would say some of the ones here they're there.
It's just a different level of opt opportunistic investing because they're not setting.
They might they're not really setting a goal for that.
I'm sure each of the businesses are setting goals that the sale requires buys.
But because Jacobs is doing this roll up strategy that's really in one industry.
It is setting different goals for for things.
But again, all companies have goals.
Some just talk about them. Some deliver on that.
I like the ones who deliver.
But I hope that the ones that don't deliver.
If I have competitors in the investing world, I hope they buy those.
In my view, the model that Jacobs has resembles sort of the private equity roll up model.
But with the key difference being that they have a perpetual holding period and private equity has a quite short holding period.
What I have seen and heard is that sort of private equity is moving out from the maybe shorter holding period in some aspects and trying to hold on to the assets for longer.
What's your view on that and do you agree on this resembling sort of private equity roll ups?
I think private equity is evolving.
I think you're absolutely right.
Not all of the companies, but I think even some of the older ones like KKR who's been around since
really long time, you'll see them.
I've seen specific cases where they buy a business.
Instead of just coming in and saying we know better, they talk to the employees.
They get to know how the business runs really well.
It's not just, as we used to say, it's not just the bean counters.
Right. The guys just looking at the numbers saying, oh, get rid of this. Get rid of that.
But they're just looking at their spreadsheets. They're not looking to the people.
Now they're talking to them. Now they're putting in bonus pools.
Now they're putting in incentives so that the people that are running the businesses or further down the line
that the employees in the factory, the warehouse, whatever happens to be, they get economic incentives.
And you see that the outcomes have been at a different level of return for them
because their more constituents get to win.
And so when you have more, you know, if I win, but the other guy has to lose,
it's not as in the long run, if you can have the buyer wins, the seller wins, the employees win, the customers win.
So if you can get the quadruple win, it's the best outcome. Everybody's happy.
It can happen. And even though you'll say, okay, most of these guys are very ruthless and aggressive.
Yes, many of them are. And that's how they've built their businesses. So I'm not critical of that.
But what I'm saying is that it seems that as the world has evolved,
sometimes you have to be very aggressive and very ruthless to get the deal done or you're not getting it done.
I mean, right now to get the, so for QXO, which is Brad Jacobs' current startup, I'll say,
he's raised more than $5 billion. He put $1 billion of his own capital to start it.
And they want to roll up the building products industry. Well, the company they want to buy doesn't want to be sold.
And so they're doing a more aggressive approach.
But it's interesting. So they're pushing to acquire it, the company's management and board are fighting.
But at the same time, he has published a letter to the employee saying, this isn't you. This is your management. This is your board.
We love you guys. We want you to be part of the future.
And so it's, it's this combination of compassion and accountability and being aggressive all in the same bucket.
And so I think some of the private equity guys are going back to your question.
Evolving some or not. They're viewers. No, I buy it at, you know, two, I sell it at four.
I used leverage. I got in. I got out. My investors are happy.
Others are thinking we can probably get maybe another turn or more on the multiple.
But they're still thinking about, see what I like about some of the cereal acquires.
They're not thinking about selling. They're thinking about buying.
All their effort is in buying. It's easy to sell a good business. You just don't want to do it.
And so it's hard to sell a bad business. Well, you want to do it. But the other person doesn't want to buy it.
And so you see because these, these groups are focused on buying, not selling.
Their whole mindset is different than the private equity, the traditional private equity guy who then before they buy, they are thinking,
what can I get for if I fix it, if I turn it around. And they're buying companies that are not always great or they've stumbled.
I've invested in companies over the years where I said, okay, it's a good business. They've stumbled. It's fixable.
And so I also look at, so I want to buy great businesses that keep compounding.
But I'll also look at companies where I say, okay, they stumbled, but I think it's fixable.
And so then you need to know who's going to do the fix. What's their track record of fixing?
Are they good at breaking, not fixing? Well, they shouldn't be in this one. Again, sell them to the competition.
Always have the weak managers go to your competition. It's the best way they can help you.
And I mean, one thing that Jacobs has really succeeded with this is sort of scaling the business, doing a lot of acquisitions.
So what do you think are sort of the main barriers to scaling because it's not so many businesses within, I mean, several acquisitions that has really succeeded in scaling at the level that Jacobs has.
They spent, I forget what he said, but it was a few years he spent before creating QXO to do this for building products.
Looking at all kinds of industries saying, where do we see highly fragmented? Maybe there's one or two larger players, but they're not enough.
They're not at a scale that dominates the whole industry. They're big. And there's so many small players that they can get in.
And then the key is if it's a very because he's attacking very large markets. He's not going for small niche markets.
He's thinking big. He's thinking beyond big mega, I don't know, whatever was bigger than bigger, bigger mega, whatever, super size.
So he's aiming so high and so maybe there are less industries that are that fragmented.
But then what do you really need to make it happen? Money. You need the capital.
